cases.why: The smallest id a row can have. The serial is zero padded to seven digits, so every code is nine long whatever the id, and a scanned string is told from an ISBN by its length alone.
The example in the design for ticket 31: lead digit 2, the id padded to 0004711, Damm check digit 6.
An id that fills most of the serial, so a runner that pads to the wrong width or drops a leading zero answers a different code.
The last id a nine digit code can carry. One more would need a tenth digit, which is an ISBN-10's length, so both sides refuse past it and this case pins the edge they agree on.
The base case: a code this app minted is one.
The last digit off by one. Damm misses no single digit error, measured over 162000 of them on nine digit codes, so a mistyped digit is refused at the desk rather than resolving to another copy.
Digits five and six of 200047116 swapped. Luhn misses 2 per cent of adjacent transpositions on these codes, measured; Damm misses none, which is why it was chosen.
Nine digits whose Damm check is sound but whose lead digit is 3. The lead digit 2 reserves the minted range, so a typed scheme added later owns the other digits and can never be read as minted.
A sound Damm check over eight digits. Eight is EAN-8's length, so a code of that length is never an accession whatever its check digit says.
A sound Damm check over ten digits, which is an ISBN-10's length. The shape is nine exactly.

200047116 with its last digit written as ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT SIX. Python's int() reads it as 6 and the check passes without an ASCII guard; JavaScript's [0-9] refuses it. The ISBN domain drifted on exactly this, so both sides refuse it here.
The predicate is exact. Stripping what a keyboard wedge adds is classify's job, so a code stored or looked up is never a padded one.
An empty scan field. Neither side may index into it or answer true.
A label this app printed names a copy.
A USB scanner in keyboard mode types the digits and then Enter. Surrounding whitespace is dropped before the code is read.
A keyboard wedge sends U+001D for a Code 128 FNC1. Python's strip() drops it and JavaScript's trim() does not, so both sides drop one pinned set: ASCII space and every C0 control.
The other half of the pinned set. JavaScript's trim() drops U+FEFF and Python's strip() does not; it is no C0 control, so neither side drops it.

Both defaults drop U+00A0, Python's strip() and JavaScript's trim() alike, so this is the case that tells either default from the pinned set. No wedge sends it, and a code pasted with one was not scanned.
Nine digits with a wrong check digit are neither a copy nor a book: no ISBN is nine long, so there is nothing to fall back to.
This app prints no separators. The ISBN parser strips hyphens, and what is left is nine digits, which is no ISBN, so a hyphenated accession is refused rather than read.
The barcode on the back of a book still means the book. An accession and an ISBN never share a length, so the two answers cannot overlap.
An ISBN-10 is ten long, one more than an accession, and it is a book.
The ISBN half is the ISBN domain's parse, hyphens included, so a typed ISBN classifies the way it would look up.
A real EAN-13 that is not Bookland: a price or a product barcode beside the ISBN. It names neither a copy nor a book.
An empty scan field is nothing, on both sides.
